sentences.text: With an army outside the walls, the city's bronze-smith spent every day laying his shield face-down in the dirt.
The guards on the wall think the siege has finally cracked him.
It's about 2,500 years ago in Barca, on the coast of Libya, and a Persian army has the city surrounded.
For months they hammer the walls, and the walls hold.
Then one week the attacks just stop, and the Persian camp goes strangely quiet.
That's when the smith starts walking the inside of the wall.
He sets his shield down, kneels, listens, then moves a few steps and does it again.
"The enemy's out there, not down there."
Just a dull thud, wherever he puts it.
Then, near the corner tower, he sets it down and it rings, and the dust on the bronze starts to shiver.
You see, the Persians had stopped attacking the wall because they were digging under it.
Over solid ground, a bronze shield just thuds.
But over a hollow tunnel, every pick striking below makes it hum like a bell.
So wherever it rang, the defenders dug straight down and broke into the tunnel from above.
An army spent months digging in total silence, and a shield lying in the dirt heard every swing.
